title: Why Do I Keep Getting Canker Sores? Causes, Deficiencies and the Blood Tests to Check
summary: Why do I keep getting canker sores? Learn the common triggers, the deficiencies and conditions linked to them, and which blood tests can find a cause.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


Most people who keep getting canker sores have no single cause that a test can find. About 1 in 5 adults has recurring canker sores at some point, the tendency runs in families, and outbreaks are usually set off by everyday triggers such as biting your cheek, stress or hormonal changes \[[1](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/dental-disorders/symptoms-of-dental-and-oral-disorders/recurrent-aphthous-stomatitis) \]\[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000998.htm) \]. Doctors call the condition recurrent aphthous stomatitis.


A smaller group has something behind the sores that a blood test can show. The usual suspects are low iron, folate or vitamin B12, less often low zinc, and conditions such as celiac disease \[[1](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/dental-disorders/symptoms-of-dental-and-oral-disorders/recurrent-aphthous-stomatitis) \]\[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000998.htm) \]\[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28613713/) \]. When sores keep returning, the Merck Manual lists a complete blood count, iron and ferritin, vitamin B12, folate and zinc among the tests to run, plus a celiac antibody test \[[4](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/dental-disorders/symptoms-of-dental-and-oral-disorders/stomatitis) \]. This page covers how to tell a canker sore from a cold sore, the common triggers, which deficiencies and conditions are linked to recurrence, which blood test matches which pattern, and when a sore needs a dentist or doctor rather than a blood test.


## Canker sore vs cold sore


Canker sores and cold sores are different conditions with different causes, and the place they appear is the quickest way to tell them apart.


Feature Canker sore Cold sore


Where Inside the mouth, on soft, movable tissue: inner cheeks, lips, tongue \[[5](https://www.aaom.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=82:aphthous-ulcers&catid=22:patient-condition-information&Itemid=120) \] On or around the lips; a first infection can also involve the gums \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000606.htm) \]


What it looks like A round, painful ulcer, white or yellow with a red border \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000998.htm) \] A cluster of small fluid-filled blisters that break and crust \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000606.htm) \]


Warning signs Pain or burning for a day or two, with no blister first \[[1](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/dental-disorders/symptoms-of-dental-and-oral-disorders/recurrent-aphthous-stomatitis) \] Itching, burning or tingling on the lip before blisters appear \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000606.htm) \]


Cause Not fully known; thought to involve the immune system \[[5](https://www.aaom.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=82:aphthous-ulcers&catid=22:patient-condition-information&Itemid=120) \] Herpes simplex virus, usually type 1 \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000606.htm) \]


Contagious No \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000998.htm) \]\[[5](https://www.aaom.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=82:aphthous-ulcers&catid=22:patient-condition-information&Itemid=120) \] Yes, spreads most easily from an open sore \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000606.htm) \]


Most canker sores are the minor type: under 8 mm across, usually 2 to 3 mm, painful for about 4 to 7 days and healed within about 10 days without a scar \[[1](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/dental-disorders/symptoms-of-dental-and-oral-disorders/recurrent-aphthous-stomatitis) \]. Major canker sores are larger than 1 cm, deeper, and can last weeks to months and scar \[[1](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/dental-disorders/symptoms-of-dental-and-oral-disorders/recurrent-aphthous-stomatitis) \]. A third type, herpetiform ulcers, appears as clusters of tiny ulcers that can merge. Despite the name, it is not caused by the herpes virus \[[1](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/dental-disorders/symptoms-of-dental-and-oral-disorders/recurrent-aphthous-stomatitis) \]\[[5](https://www.aaom.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=82:aphthous-ulcers&catid=22:patient-condition-information&Itemid=120) \].


## Common triggers for canker sores


Canker sores are thought to start when white blood cells briefly attack the lining of the mouth \[[5](https://www.aaom.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=82:aphthous-ulcers&catid=22:patient-condition-information&Itemid=120) \]. The reason is not fully known, but several triggers come up again and again:


- **Mouth injuries,** such as biting your cheek or tongue, dental work or rough brushing \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000998.htm) \].
- **Emotional stress** \[[1](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/dental-disorders/symptoms-of-dental-and-oral-disorders/recurrent-aphthous-stomatitis) \]\[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000998.htm) \].
- **Hormonal changes** \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000998.htm) \].
- **Stopping smoking** \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28613713/) \].
- **Foods and toothpaste.** Some people react to food ingredients or to components of toothpaste and mouthwash \[[5](https://www.aaom.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=82:aphthous-ulcers&catid=22:patient-condition-information&Itemid=120) \]. Chocolate, peanuts and eggs may worsen sores for some, although studies have not shown that food allergy causes the condition \[[1](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/dental-disorders/symptoms-of-dental-and-oral-disorders/recurrent-aphthous-stomatitis) \].
- **Family history.** Up to 46% of people with recurring canker sores report a relative with them \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28613713/) \], and women get them more often than men \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000998.htm) \].


Sores that follow these triggers, heal within about 10 days and leave long gaps between outbreaks fit the common pattern. They do not need a blood workup on their own.


## Deficiencies linked to recurring canker sores


Low iron, folic acid and vitamin B12 are linked to canker sores \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000998.htm) \], and the Merck Manual adds zinc and other B vitamins, while noting that isolated recurring sores only rarely come from a deficiency \[[1](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/dental-disorders/symptoms-of-dental-and-oral-disorders/recurrent-aphthous-stomatitis) \]. It also notes that correcting a deficiency of iron, folate, B12 or other B vitamins lessens the sores in some patients \[[1](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/dental-disorders/symptoms-of-dental-and-oral-disorders/recurrent-aphthous-stomatitis) \]. That is the practical reason to check: a deficiency is one of the few causes of recurring canker sores that has a specific fix.


A deficiency is more likely when there is a reason for one:


- **Iron:** heavy, long or frequent periods, other ongoing blood loss, a diet low in iron-rich foods, pregnancy, or a gut that does not absorb iron well \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000584.htm) \].
- **Vitamin B12:** older age, a vegetarian or vegan diet, pernicious anemia, a digestive disorder or past stomach or bowel surgery, or long-term use of metformin or proton pump inhibitors \[[8](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminB12-HealthProfessional/) \]. A sore, swollen tongue (glossitis) is one recognized sign of low B12 \[[8](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminB12-HealthProfessional/) \].
- **Folate:** too little folate in the diet, long-term heavy alcohol use, a problem with the intestines, or some medicines such as methotrexate and phenytoin \[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000551.htm) \].
- **Zinc:** heavy alcohol use, a digestive condition that affects absorption, or a vegetarian or vegan diet \[[10](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Zinc-HealthProfessional/) \].


The same deficiencies can come from celiac disease or inflammatory bowel disease, which reduce how well the gut absorbs nutrients. That is one reason the celiac test sits on the same list.


## Conditions linked to recurring canker sores


Recurring mouth ulcers can be part of a wider condition. These conditions usually cause other symptoms too, which is the clue that the sores are not the whole story \[[1](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/dental-disorders/symptoms-of-dental-and-oral-disorders/recurrent-aphthous-stomatitis) \].


- **Celiac disease.** Canker sores are one of the mouth problems celiac disease can cause \[[11](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/celiac-disease/diagnosis) \]. Bloating, diarrhea, weight loss or unexplained low iron add weight to the question.
- **Inflammatory bowel disease.** Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis are linked to mouth ulcers \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28613713/) \]. Look for ongoing diarrhea, belly pain, blood in the stool or weight loss.
- **Behçet disease.** Painful mouth ulcers are usually its first sign. About 75% of people with it also get ulcers on the genitals, and it can affect the skin and eyes \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/behcet-disease/) \].
- **HIV.** Unusually severe canker sores can be a sign of HIV infection \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28613713/) \].
- **Cyclic neutropenia.** A rare inherited condition, found in about 1 in 1 million people, in which the neutrophil count drops every 21 days or so for 3 to 5 days. Mouth ulcers, sore throat and fever tend to come back on the same cycle \[[13](https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/cyclic-neutropenia/) \]. For what a low count means, see our article on[low neutrophils on a CBC](https://mitohealth.com/blog/low-neutrophils-causes) .


If you also keep getting colds and other infections, our article on[why you keep getting sick](https://mitohealth.com/blog/why-do-i-keep-getting-sick) covers the blood tests that look for a reason.


## Medicines that can cause mouth ulcers


Some medicines cause mouth ulcers that look like canker sores. They usually start soon after the medicine does \[[1](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/dental-disorders/symptoms-of-dental-and-oral-disorders/recurrent-aphthous-stomatitis) \]. The Merck Manual lists chemotherapy as a common cause, and antibiotics, antiseizure medicines, barbiturates, gold, iodides and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) as rare ones. Aspirin held against the gum or cheek can also burn the lining \[[4](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/dental-disorders/symptoms-of-dental-and-oral-disorders/stomatitis) \]. If sores started after a new medicine, raise it with the clinician who prescribed it rather than stopping it on your own.


## Which blood tests check for a cause


Blood tests do not test the sore itself. They check whether something in your blood points to a cause that can be treated. The table maps each pattern to the test to start with, what the test can show and what a normal result cannot rule out.


Pattern Test to start with What it can show What a normal result cannot rule out


Frequent sores with tiredness, pale skin, or fevers[CBC with differential and platelet count](https://mitohealth.com/products/complete-blood-count-cbc-with-differential-and-platelet-count) Anemia, large or small red cells, a low neutrophil count Low iron stores before anemia sets in, or cyclic neutropenia between dips


Heavy periods, a low-iron diet, or tiredness[Ferritin](https://mitohealth.com/products/ferritin) Low iron stores Low iron during an infection or inflammation, which raises ferritin


Vegan diet, older age, metformin, a sore tongue, or numb hands or feet[Vitamin B12 and Folate Panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/vitamin-b12-cobalamin-and-folate-panel) Low B12 or folate Early B12 deficiency when the level is borderline


Heavy alcohol use or a digestive condition[Zinc](https://mitohealth.com/products/zinc) Low blood zinc Low body zinc, because blood levels shift with timing and illness


Bloating, diarrhea, weight loss, or unexplained low iron[Celiac Disease Panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/celiac-disease-panel) (tTG-IgA with total IgA), while still eating gluten Celiac antibodies, and whether IgA is too low to trust them Celiac disease if you had already cut out gluten before the test


If you want one draw for the deficiency questions, the[Anemia Panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/anemia-panel-b) combines a complete blood count, full iron studies including ferritin, vitamin B12 and folate. It does not include zinc or celiac antibodies.


### Complete blood count: anemia and white cells


A complete blood count measures red cells, white cells and platelets. It is used to look for anemia, infections and immune and blood disorders \[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/complete-blood-count-cbc/) \]. For recurring canker sores, it answers two questions in one draw: whether you are anemic, and whether your neutrophils, the white cells that fight infection, are low. Red cell size adds a clue. Small red cells point toward low iron, and large ones toward low B12 or folate. A[complete blood count with differential and platelet count](https://mitohealth.com/products/complete-blood-count-cbc-with-differential-and-platelet-count) gives the full breakdown.


Where it stops: an abnormal result does not always mean you have a condition that needs treatment \[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/complete-blood-count-cbc/) \], and a normal one does not mean your iron, B12 or folate stores are full. The count can stay normal while stores run down. In cyclic neutropenia the count drops for only 3 to 5 days of each cycle of about 21 days \[[13](https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/cyclic-neutropenia/) \], so one normal count taken between dips does not rule it out.


### Ferritin: iron stores


Ferritin reflects how much iron your body has stored, and a low result points to iron deficiency \[[15](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/ferritin-blood-test/) \]. It often drops before the hemoglobin on a complete blood count does, which is why it belongs on the list even when the count looks normal. A[ferritin blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/ferritin) measures it on its own. For what the marker measures, see[ferritin](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/ferritin) , and for how to read a result, see our[ferritin level guide](https://mitohealth.com/guide/ferritin-level) .


Where it stops: inflammation, such as from an infection or surgery, raises ferritin \[[15](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/ferritin-blood-test/) \], so a normal result during an inflammatory illness can hide low stores.


### Vitamin B12 and folate


Vitamin B12 and folate are often measured together, because both are needed to make healthy blood cells and both are checked when anemia is a question \[[16](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/vitamin-b-test/) \]. The[Vitamin B12 and Folate Panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/vitamin-b12-cobalamin-and-folate-panel) covers both in one draw. If only one is in question, the[vitamin B12 blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/vitamin-b12-cobalamin) and the[folate blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/folate-folic-acid) measure them separately. For what each marker does, see[vitamin B12](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/vitamin-b12) and[folate](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/folate) .


Where it stops: the cutoff between normal and low B12 varies by laboratory, and a borderline result may need a follow-up test called methylmalonic acid (MMA), the most sensitive marker of B12 status \[[8](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminB12-HealthProfessional/) \]. Inflammation and some medicines also affect B vitamin results. If your levels are normal and the symptoms continue, other tests may be needed \[[16](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/vitamin-b-test/) \].


### Zinc


Blood zinc is the standard way to check zinc status in practice \[[10](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Zinc-HealthProfessional/) \]. A[zinc blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/zinc) is most useful when there is a reason for low zinc, such as heavy alcohol use or a digestive condition that affects absorption. For what zinc does, see[zinc](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/zinc) .


Where it stops: blood zinc has important limits. It varies with sex, age and the time of day of the draw, does not always match how much zinc you take in, and shifts with infections, hormones and illness \[[10](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Zinc-HealthProfessional/) \]. One result, low or normal, is one piece of evidence.


### Celiac Disease Panel: tTG-IgA with total IgA


The tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA) test is the preferred first blood test for celiac disease \[[17](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/professionals/clinical-tools-patient-management/digestive-diseases/celiac-disease-health-care-professionals) \]. About 2% to 3% of people with celiac disease have IgA deficiency, and in them IgA-based tests such as tTG-IgA may miss the disease. Measuring total IgA alongside tTG-IgA shows whether the result can be trusted \[[17](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/professionals/clinical-tools-patient-management/digestive-diseases/celiac-disease-health-care-professionals) \]. The[Celiac Disease Panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/celiac-disease-panel) measures both.


Where it stops: the test is accurate only while you are eating gluten \[[17](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/professionals/clinical-tools-patient-management/digestive-diseases/celiac-disease-health-care-professionals) \]. Keep eating foods that contain gluten for a few weeks before testing \[[18](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/celiac-disease-screening/) \], and do not start a gluten-free diet before you are tested \[[11](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/celiac-disease/diagnosis) \]. A negative result means you probably do not have celiac disease \[[18](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/celiac-disease-screening/) \]. A positive one is not a diagnosis on its own, and usually leads to further testing. Our guide on[how to test for celiac disease](https://mitohealth.com/guide/how-to-test-for-celiac-disease) explains the full pathway.


For a wider look at anemia and its causes, see our[anemia test guide](https://mitohealth.com/guide/anemia-test) .


## When a mouth sore needs a dentist or doctor instead


A blood test does not rule out oral cancer. Mouth cancer is found by examining the mouth and taking a sample of any suspicious area, not by a blood test \[[19](https://www.nidcr.nih.gov/health-info/oral-cancer) \]\[[20](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/ear,-nose,-and-throat-disorders/tumors-of-the-head-and-neck/oral-squamous-cell-carcinoma) \]. See a dentist or doctor if a sore or other change in your mouth:


- has not healed after about 2 weeks \[[19](https://www.nidcr.nih.gov/health-info/oral-cancer) \]. Ordinary canker sores usually heal within 1 to 3 weeks \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000998.htm) \]
- does not hurt, or feels hard or firm. Early mouth cancers are often painless, and they are often firm to the touch \[[20](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/ear,-nose,-and-throat-disorders/tumors-of-the-head-and-neck/oral-squamous-cell-carcinoma) \]
- is a white or red patch, a lump, or a thick patch in the mouth, lip or throat \[[19](https://www.nidcr.nih.gov/health-info/oral-cancer) \]
- comes with numbness in the tongue or mouth, or a lump in the neck \[[19](https://www.nidcr.nih.gov/health-info/oral-cancer) \]


Contact a doctor too if sores come with fever, diarrhea, headache or a skin rash, if they come back more than 2 or 3 times a year \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000998.htm) \], or if you almost always have one, or have tiredness, belly pain, eye discomfort or sores elsewhere on the body \[[5](https://www.aaom.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=82:aphthous-ulcers&catid=22:patient-condition-information&Itemid=120) \]. Those patterns point toward the conditions above, where an exam matters as much as the blood tests.


## How to prevent canker sores from coming back


There is no guaranteed way to prevent canker sores \[[5](https://www.aaom.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=82:aphthous-ulcers&catid=22:patient-condition-information&Itemid=120) \], but a few steps reduce the common triggers:


- **Keep an ulcer diary.** Note each outbreak alongside foods, toothpaste, stress and your cycle, and share it with your dentist or doctor \[[5](https://www.aaom.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=82:aphthous-ulcers&catid=22:patient-condition-information&Itemid=120) \].
- **Try a toothpaste without sodium lauryl sulfate.** Some people have fewer outbreaks after switching \[[5](https://www.aaom.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=82:aphthous-ulcers&catid=22:patient-condition-information&Itemid=120) \].
- **Avoid mouth injury.** Brush gently, and ask your dentist to check sharp teeth or dental work that rubs \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000998.htm) \].
- **Skip hot or spicy foods** while a sore heals, because they make it hurt more \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000998.htm) \].
- **Fix a deficiency if testing finds one,** with a clinician deciding how, rather than taking supplements on a guess.

## Frequently asked questions


### What deficiency causes canker sores?


Low iron, folate and vitamin B12 are the deficiencies most often linked to canker sores, and low zinc and other B vitamins are linked less often. A deficiency explains only a minority of cases, so most people with recurring canker sores have normal levels. A complete blood count, ferritin, B12, folate and zinc are the blood tests used to look for one.


### Are canker sores a sign of a weak immune system?


On their own, usually not. Canker sores are thought to start when white blood cells briefly attack the lining of the mouth, and the conditions linked to them usually cause other symptoms too. Sores that are unusually large, severe or constant are different. They can go with conditions that affect immunity, such as HIV or cyclic neutropenia, and are a reason to see a doctor.


### Can stress cause canker sores?


Stress is one of the recognized triggers. Emotional stress, mouth injuries such as biting your cheek, hormonal changes and stopping smoking are all linked to outbreaks in people who are prone to them. Stress does not explain every case, so frequent sores still deserve a look for other causes.


### Are canker sores contagious?


No. Canker sores cannot spread from person to person through kissing or sharing a cup. Cold sores are different: they are caused by the herpes simplex virus and spread easily, especially while a blister is open.


### Can toothpaste cause canker sores?


For some people, yes. Many toothpastes contain sodium lauryl sulfate, a foaming detergent, and some people with recurring canker sores have fewer outbreaks after switching to a toothpaste without it. Others notice no change. Keeping a diary of outbreaks is the simplest way to tell.


### Is it normal to get canker sores every month?


Some people prone to canker sores get them that often, and hormonal changes are one recognized trigger. Frequent sores are still worth raising with a doctor or dentist, who suggest a visit when sores come back more than 2 or 3 times a year, or when you almost always have one.
